edges.rationale: Channel partitioning is presented as one solution class to the collision problem; understanding why collisions occur motivates dividing the channel.
Slotted ALOHA is the simplest random access protocol designed to cope with collisions; the problem statement defines what its efficiency analysis measures.
CSMA improves on random access by reducing collisions; the collision problem and collision interval concept are needed to understand carrier sensing and backoff.
Taking-turns protocols are a third class of solutions to the multiple access problem; the problem frames why coordination via polling or tokens is needed.
CSMA is introduced as an evolution of ALOHA-style random access; slotted ALOHA's efficiency analysis provides the baseline that carrier sensing improves upon.
DOCSIS uses FDM to divide downstream and upstream channels, directly applying the channel partitioning concept.
DOCSIS upstream transmission is regulated by the CMTS granting permissions to modems, which is a polling-style taking-turns mechanism.
The DOCSIS case study explicitly combines the three multiple access classes, so the framing problem must be understood first.
